items.title: codex 0.169.0
items.summary:
New Features

  • The opt-in terminal workspace supports multiple side-chat tabs. Switch between them with the keyboard or mouse, and reopen saved local side chats after restarting Codex. (#59784, #60152, #60181)
  • Search older tasks from the agent command center by name, prompt preview, or working directory. (#60286)
  • Turn on Collapse turn details in the full-screen transcript to fold completed activity beneath each prompt while keeping answers visible and tool output searchable. (#60554, #60555, #60556, #60557)
  • Add or edit custom model providers from the terminal. With custom gateway onboarding enabled, you can create a provider during sign-in and use a device code for supported gateways over SSH or without a local browser. (#59779, #60009, #60186, #60486, #60662)
  • Press Ctrl+S in the terminal report editor to save a diagnostic ZIP locally, even when uploads are disabled. (#60542)
  • With the opt-in Cloud connection on macOS and Linux, send images, choose a model and reasoning effort, and archive or restore Cloud conversations from the terminal. (#59828, #60061, #60635, #60651)

Bug Fixes

  • codex exec keeps project configuration and MCP servers disabled in untrusted directories, even with --sandbox workspace-write. Use --trust with codex exec or codex review to explicitly save project trust. (#60041)
  • Yes, clear context and implement now hands the full approved plan to the fresh session and keeps the current session open if the handoff fails. (#60763)
  • Fixed Windows sandbox handling for quoted cmd.exe paths and for PowerShell sessions whose working directory has an unreadable parent. (#60624, #60647)
  • Pasted images on macOS retain their intended orientation and use native PNG or JPEG clipboard data when available. (#60455)
  • The terminal no longer stays busy waiting for MCP servers that a shared app server did not report. (#60280, #60622)
  • Interrupted turns now close cleanly, and delayed aborts or file approval cancellations no longer interrupt a later turn. (#59910, #60700)

Documentation

  • Updated the openai-docs skill to focus on Codex and ChatGPT Work questions and first-time API setup, with dedicated guidance for configuring Codex across a team. (#59944, #59949)
  • Documented how app-server clients can list models or authorize a gateway for a configured provider without changing the default provider. (#59776, #59819)

Chores

  • Updated bundled SQLite to 3.54 to pick up write-ahead log fixes. (#60432)
  • Plugin marketplace upgrades can reuse Git objects already on disk, reducing repeat downloads. (#60528)

items.title: JudgeMix: Judge-Guided Mixed-Rollout Data Synthesis for LLM Agents
items.summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories is a standard paradigm for training LLM agents. However, it suffers from a well-known training-inference distribution mismatch, calling for target-aware data synthesis strategies that ground the training data in the target model's native state distribution. To bridge this gap, emerging approaches incorporate the expert either to guide mixed rollouts alongside the target model, or to provide dense step-wise supervision. Nonetheless, existing methods apply expert assistance blind to the target model's inherent behavior: they either disrupt the rollout using sub-optimal random intervention heuristics, or they enforce indiscriminate uniform supervision that unnecessarily overwrites the model's already-correct actions. We introduce JudgeMix, a judge-guided data synthesis framework that dynamically interleaves the target model and expert based on step-wise semantic evaluations. JudgeMix queries expert guidance precisely when the target model struggles, ensuring high trajectory success rates while keeping the state distribution aligned with the target model. It additionally uses the judge evaluation to reweight expert supervision on different steps, preserving model's inherent valid behavior while correcting its errors. On two agentic tool-use benchmarks, AppWorld and AutomationBench, JudgeMix demonstrates consistent superior performance to existing methods, with improvements up to 10 pass@1 points.

items.title: S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models
items.summary: Typed System-1 (S1) decision models are increasingly deployed in LLM agents for routing, moderation, and authorization to cut inference cost, yet untrusted context can still manipulate typed outputs and alter execution branches. Unlike autoregressive System-2 (S2) models, S1 interfaces score dynamic rules and options without token-by-token decoding, mismatching attacks targeting text continuation or explicit override commands. We propose S1-Evo, a self-evolving framework tailored to S1's contract-based option competition and margin feedback. S1-Evo perturbs untrusted fields via contract-aware evidence channels to induce \emph{evidence competition} with original task evidence while preserving fact invariance. Offline on seed tasks, it optimizes candidates via feedback search guided by directional margins and re-verification, distilling verified flips into experience cards. At test time, S1-Evo retrieves relevant cards to construct perturbations for unseen tasks. Across four benchmarks and three S1 models, S1-Evo reaches 71.99\% mean ASR and 57.47\% high-confidence ASR on \texttt{jev-1.14}, and causes up to 24.00\% E2E agent violations.

items.title: We Are What We Remember: Mental-State-Driven Memory for Long-Term Character Dialogue
items.summary: Shared history in human dialogue is not merely a repository of facts, but the foundation of evolving relationships and mutual understanding. However, mainstream conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over external fact stores, frequently retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences. Inspired by cognitive psychology's Self-Memory System (SMS), we propose MindMem, a mental-state-driven memory framework that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into source-linked mental states of the character, the user, and their relationship. At each turn, a specialized mental-state reasoner (Mind) contextualizes these persistent states to anticipate latent user needs, form proactive intentions, and recover supporting episodic evidence that surface-level matching overlooks. To evaluate history-sensitive adaptation beyond factual recall, we introduce MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark grounded in month-long real-user interactions across dyadic and group scenes. By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/jiazhicheng7-ctrl/MindMem.

items.story_key: model:langgraph|title:how workday built an enterprise scale ai agent platform with langgraph and langs
items.content_excerpt: Workday is the trusted agentic platform for HR, finance, and IT, serving more than half the Fortune 500. The team set out to create the internal developer platform to build, deploy, and run AI agents in production, on Workday's infrastructure. The team leveraged LangGraph for agent orchestration and LangSmith for tracing, observability, and evals. In 2025, Workday’s leadership team saw the market opportunity for building agentic solutions and set an ambitious goal for agents in production by the end of 2026. Product teams needed a platform that could support both rapid prototyping and production deployments—a uniquely challenging mandate given Workday operates under some of the strictest security and data governance requirements in enterprise software. Getting any internal service into production means satisfying demanding audit, compliance, and data retention policies. The surface area was enormous for a team of four, encompassing a durable, scalable agent server; data access controls tied to Workday's audit policies; a collaborative eval platform; and an SDK that abstracted all of it. Workday’s Agent Platform team serves two user bases. 1.) the internal Workday engineering teams building agents, and 2.) the end customers of those agents. It lets teams focus on functional requirements, while handling authentication, security, compliance, and infrastructure. The first major product shipped was Workday's Agent System of Record, a governance layer that controls which APIs the agents are allowed to access. The Agent Platform team built the backend server and eval infrastructure that the system of record runs on top of. The team also built what Alex Gatto, Senior Machine Learning Engineer, describes as "Workday LangChain": a Python SDK that wraps LangChain primitives and routes them through Workday's internal services, including an LLM gateway, a RAG retrieval service, and other internal tooling. "Anytime there was some AI concept that LangChain had put out, we tried to build a Python SDK for that same concept, but at Workday," explained Alex. Workday chose LangGraph for agent orchestration to give internal developers maximum flexibility at the design layer, while providing standardized infrastructure underneath. items.title: The Iron(wood) Throne: Google's TPU Stakes Its Claim on Inference
items.summary: Viable Alternative of CUDA Moat, NVIDIA scared and working nights & weekends, Jensen’s Counter Submission, Kimi K3, Muse Spark Open, Qwen, GLM5.3, TorchTPU, vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, Ray
items.story_key: story|title:the iron wood throne google s tpu stakes its claim on inference
items.content_excerpt: In November 2025, we published a newsletter saying that Google is selling TPUs to external customers. Since then, we have been proven right over and over again with Oracle, OpenAI , Anthropic, and Meta all becoming customers of TPUs just as our Accelerator Model reported. Hardware demand is only half the story, as NVIDIA’s moat has historically been its software and large developer ecosystem. This is where TPU is also making headway, partnering with upstream maintainers across the entire ecosystem, including the Meta PyTorch team, vLLM (Inferact, RedHat), SGLang (RadixArk), llm-d, Ray, etc. This is not a surprise to folks that have read our September 2026 article laying out Google TPU’s externalization strategy . Back in our September article, we published the first third-party TPUv7 results on InferenceX on single-turn workloads, showing that in an apples-to-apples FP8 comparison on Qwen 3.5 397B, TPUv7 Ironwood) delivered up to 50% better performance per dollar than B200 and B300. We also reported that many Google TPU customers were asking for AgentX results, since long-context, multi-turn agentic serving is where inference spend is heading. Previously, Jensen went on the Dwarkesh Podcast and commented on the fact that no other chips were taking advantage of their opportunity to show performance on InferenceX. Six months later, and indeed Google is taking full advantage of this opportunity. Today we are releasing the first official long-context, multi-turn, realistic agentic inference benchmark results on TPUv7 across four models, showing that TPUv7 is either competitive on perf per dollar for external customers or delivers the best state-of-the-art result: Muse Spark Open SGLang AgentX (NVFP4 weights): Competitive TPU performance per dollar result even though the architecture was co-designed for GPUs. Submitted by OSS ecosystem developer, RadixArk (Makers of SGLang). GLM-5.2 vLLM AgentX (FP8): TPUv7 is the cheapest FP8 option, delivering 1.2x to 2.7x the tokens per dollar of B200, B300, and MI355X from 60 to 300 tok/s/user. NVIDIA NVFP4 still beats TPUv7 FP8, but with accuracy / quality loss. Qwen3.5 vLLM AgentX (FP8): With llm-d disaggregated serving, TPUv7 beats GB300 FP8 at every interactivity level and restores parity even against GB300 FP4 at higher quality / accuracy. Kimi K3 vLLM AgentX (MXFP4 weights): Competitive with GB300 NVL72 at launch; With TPUv7 delivering 1.15x to 2.5x the tokens per dollar of GB200, B200, B300, and MI355X. Submitted by

items.title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers
items.summary: LLM-based peer review is now used at production scale, but its evaluation remains limited. We introduce a benchmark that injects objective, localisable errors of four types (general issues, mathematics, numerics, citations) at three severity levels into real papers and measures each reviewer's detection rate by error type and severity, together with its false-positive rate on clean copies. We also present Skepthical, a multi-agent reviewer that verifies citation-backed claims by retrieving the cited papers, mathematics with computer algebra, and numerical claims with executed code. We apply the benchmark to two corpora of 15 recent arXiv preprints each, one in astrophysics and one in machine learning (ML), injecting a total of 357 errors, and evaluate twelve reviewer systems: six single-LLM reviewers, two Claude Code configurations, three publicly available reviewers, and Skepthical. The choice of model has the largest impact on detection rate: given the same prompt, three frontier LLMs differ by about 50 percentage points in total detection on both corpora. Tools and scaffolding help when they contribute what the model cannot supply on its own. In particular, on astrophysics, Claude Code improves on a single Claude call in mathematics and numerics detection, and enforced citation retrieval gives Skepthical the highest citation error detection rate of all systems by a large margin. This citation lead, however, is not observed on ML, where the models appear to know the literature better and Skepthical's citation detection rate is statistically indistinguishable from that of the best single LLM. False-positive rates are below 10% for most systems, but vary with prompt, model, and scaffolding, with mathematics flags the main source of false positives. The evaluation pipeline, the injected errors, and the adjudication logs are released as a benchmark.

items.title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
items.summary: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.
